newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arthuis says dollar gains should be lasting - paper.
newsitem.headline: Arthuis says dollar gains should be lasting - paper.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said in a French newspaper interview that the dollar's rise has been good, and the new exchange rate parities should be stable and lasting.

"This recovery of the dollar is a good thing, it was logical and necessary," Arthuis told the newspaper Le Journal de Dimanche, which appears on news stands on Sunday. Extracts of the interview were sent to Reuters.
"It's a good thing for growth and for jobs, in France and in Europe, which have suffered too much in recent years from the weakness in the U.S. currency," he was quoted as saying.
"But this new parity should be durable and stable. What's harmful for growth and destroys jobs is monetary instability," Arthuis said.
Arthuis was interviewes in Berlin, where he was attending a meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations.

Asked whether the G7 found the dollar to be at a good level, Arthuis said "yes, I consider that it's a good equilibrium. Certainly, the Japanese worry about the yen becoming too weak, but the European currencies remained stable relative to one another in the face of this rise in the dollar, and that's very encouraging for the future of Europe."
Arthuis dismissed suggestions the dollar's evolution resulted from former French President Valery Giscard d'Estaing's call late last year for a French franc depreciation.
Giscard d'Estaing said the French unit was too strong against the dollar because of the long-standing insistence on pegging the franc to the German mark.

"Could we have, as he suggested, devalued the franc relative to the mark? Since April 1995, the G7 members had continually denounced the weakness of the dollar," Arthuis said. "I was constantly recalling the need for its revaluation. We've finally arrived there without putting at risk the equilibrium of the European currencies."
Asked what the G7 thought of the euro, Europe's future single currency scheduled to be launched in 1999, Arthuis said "that it's becoming a reality."
